title: Lengthen a paint-roller pole for a ceiling: counter-twist its loose tubes to free the twist lock, set the mark, relock
instruction: Twist the pole's tubes against each other to free its lock, set it to the red mark, and lock it again.
context: Painting a room's ceiling with a roller: before rolling it, a person lengthens the roller's extension pole and locks it. The pole here is a real one, a Mr. LongArm 9224 Twist-Lok (2.3 to 4 ft, anodized aluminium), sold for painting, staining and dusting; its internal lock locks with a twist at any length. Most people who have painted a room know this step first-hand. The lock frees and wedges with a quarter turn of the inner tube against the outer. The pole lies loose on the table, and a round tube hardly resists rolling, so a twist on one tube rolls the whole pole unless the other tube is held still at the same moment. Then a draw sets the length without dragging the outer tube, and a turn back locks it. The lock has no detent, click or hole: only a push along the pole shows it is locked.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of the table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A Mr. LongArm 9224 Twist-Lok extension pole (2.3 to 4 ft, anodized aluminium, nylon threaded end) lies on the table along y at x 40, collapsed to 70 cm: a 1 in (25.4 mm) outer tube, 64 cm long, its capped end at y 49 and its collar at y -15, and a 22 mm inner tube coming out of the collar towards the right arm, its threaded tip at y -21. A red band 10 mm wide is painted on the inner tube 24 cm from the collar: hidden inside the outer tube while the pole is collapsed, it comes out at the collar's edge when the pole reads 94 cm, the ceiling setting. A yellow index stripe runs along the inner tube from the collar (about 20 mm shows while collapsed), to read its turn by. The pole weighs about 0.47 kg and starts locked.
scoring: Tape and a push. The cam counts as locked when the inner tube is turned back within 20 degrees of where it was found. At the end, the pole on the table: the red band within 10 mm of the outer tube's collar (the pole 93 to 95 cm long), and the cam locked. Then, with both grippers 3 cm clear of the pole, a push of 50 N along the pole for 2 s, the outer tube's end held: it shortens under 2 mm. 1.0: all of these. 0.5: at the mark but not locked, or locked at the mark and it shortens 2 mm or more under the push. 0.25: locked within 30 mm of the mark. Without the push (a gripper still within 3 cm of the pole), the best is 0.25. 0: off the table, not extended at least 20 mm, or anything else. Real trial: a tape; then stand the pole on its outer tube's capped end on a bathroom scale, press the inner tube's tip down to 5 kg (about 50 N) for 2 s, and read the tape again: it must shorten under 2 mm. A real lock may hold at any angle, so in the real trial 'locked' is judged by this push for every tier.
reset_notes: The pole collapsed to 70 cm and locked, laid on the table along y at x 40 cm with its cap at y 49 cm. No seed changes the scene.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz on GPU. The cam is a stated coupling: within 20 degrees of as found the slide holds up to 200 N, at 70 degrees either way it slides at 2 N, linear between; turning it takes 0.3 N m (our guess, not measured). Tubes are hulls of 32 sides. The push holds the outer tube's end as a floor would.
